Additive manufacturing, more commonly known as 3D printing, offers a compelling pathway toward achieving this goal. Laboratory-scale studies demonstrate that printed flumes can be produced at very low cost while reproducing the internal geometries and accurate discharge relationships required for open-channel flow measurement

, for example, evaluated 0.122-m HS and 0.102-m Palmer–Bowlus flumes printed in polylactic acid (PLA) and polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG), showing remarkably consistent performance across materials and replications, with adjusted R² values exceeding 97% for all tested configurations. A 95% HPDI represents the range of parameter values that contains 95% of the posterior probability mass, given the observed data and model assumptions. In practical terms, this means that, conditional on the data collected during flume calibration and the specified model, there is a 95% probability that the true parameter value, such as a rating-curve coefficient in
, lies within this interval. This interpretation follows directly from the Bayesian framework, where uncertainty is expressed as probability over unknown quantities.

By contrast, a 95% confidence interval is defined in terms of repeated sampling. Specifically, if the same experiment, such as the stage–discharge testing described in this study, were repeated many times, 95% of the constructed intervals would contain the true parameter value. However, for any single dataset, the confidence interval does not permit a direct probabilistic statement about the parameter itself. The parameter is treated as fixed, and the interval is random, which makes interpretation less intuitive in applied settings.

The fiberglass flume exhibits a steeper posterior median curvature parameter and wider posterior intervals relative to the printed units. Similarly, while the posterior scale parameters (a) for the printed flumes cluster tightly around the expected magnitude, the fiberglass flume shows greater dispersion. However, this greater uncertainty should be interpreted in light of the smaller calibration dataset (n = 4) available for the fiberglass flume compared to each 3D

printed flume (n = 6). In a Bayesian framework, posterior distribution dispersion naturally reflects both data variability and information content; with fewer observations spanning the stage range, the model has less constraint on the curvature and scale parameters. Consequently, wider

s for the fiberglass unit are expected under limited sample support and do not necessarily imply inferior hydraulic performance. With additional calibration points for the fiberglass flume, one would expect its posterior intervals to contract, potentially reducing apparent differences in curvature.

A principal advantage of the Bayesian framework in this context is its explicit characterization of uncertainty in both parameters and predicted discharge. Rather than treating discharge observations as error-free, the model separates measurement error from structural hydraulic variability. Specifically, observed discharge was modeled as arising from a latent “true” discharge variable, with proportional measurement error and additive process variance estimated directly from the data. The use of latent true discharge variables further enhances interpretation of

, where filled points represent posterior estimates of the underlying hydraulic discharge after accounting for measurement noise. These points are what the parameters were calibrated to: not the raw data. This distinction allows separation of instrument variability from physical rating-curve behavior, which is not possible in a simple least-squares framework.
This approach was particularly well suited to the relatively small number of calibration points per flume (n = 4–6). Classical nonlinear regression quantifies parameter uncertainty using asymptotic
normal theory, which assumes that parameter estimates approach a bell-shaped distribution as sample size increases

uch asymptotic results are approximations whose accuracy depends on sufficient sample size. When data are limited, these normal approximations may not hold, and linearized standard errors derived from them can misrepresent true uncertainty or produce unstable coefficient estimates. In contrast, Bayesian inference does not rely on asymptotic normality for uncertainty quantification. Instead, it derives full posterior distributions directly from the likelihood and prior, allowing parameter uncertainty, measurement error, and process variability to be jointly propagated through the rating curve even when data are sparse

This distinction is particularly valuable for laboratory flume calibration studies, where collecting large numbers of stage–discharge observations may be impractical and where overconfidence in standard errors could lead to misleading discharge estimates

results demonstrate that the Bayesian model not only provided stable parameter estimates under limited data but also delivered a mechanistic decomposition of uncertainty into measurement error, process variability, and structural curvature differences. These findings align with prior work demonstrating that properly fabricated 3D

printed flumes can reproduce discharge relationships with high consistency and minimal between-print variability, while highlighting the additional inferential clarity gained through probabilistic modeling
Beyond parameter estimation, the practical utility of the Bayesian framework is demonstrated through the generative model aspect of the approach by creating stage–discharge predictions summarized in

. Results translate the calibrated rating curves into directly usable discharge estimates across the operational depth range, with full uncertainty propagation. This is particularly important for applied water-measurement contexts, where decisions are often made at specific stage thresholds. For example, at h = 0.5 ft, both 3D

printed flumes produce median predictions within 0.06 CFS of the manufacturer equation, while the fiberglass flume exhibits lower median discharge and wider uncertainty bounds. In applied irrigation and compliance settings, therefore provides a probabilistic

discharge lookup framework that is more informative than a single power-law curve, enabling practitioners to quantify both expected flow and associated uncertainty at any stage within the tested range.

Many professionals are exploring alternative lower-cost options because of cost constraints, and research and development is largely focused on in situ sensors that produce high temporal resolution data. While some guidance is available, contemporary information is needed to balance water quality monitoring decisions with financial and personnel constraints, while meeting data quality needs. This manuscript focuses on monitoring constituents, such as sediment, nutrients, and pathogens, at the field scale and in small watersheds. Specifically, the impacts on the costs and data quality of alternatives related to site selection, discharge measurement, and constituent concentration measurement, are explored. The present analysis showed that avoiding sites requiring extensive berm construction and the installation of electric power to reach distant sites greatly reduces the initial costs with little impact on data quality; however, other decisions directly impact data quality. For example, proper discharge measurement, high-frequency sampling, frequent site and equipment maintenance, and the purchase of backup power and monitoring equipment can be costly, but are important for high quality data collection. In contrast, other decisions such as the equipment type (mechanical samplers, electronic samplers, or in situ sensors) and whether to analyze discrete or composite samples greatly affect the costs, but have minimal impact on data quality. These decisions, therefore, can be based on other considerations (e.g., project goals, intended data uses, funding agency specifications, and agency protocols). ASABE","DOI":"10.13031/trans.14365","ISSN":"21510040","issued":{"date-parts":[[2021]]},"page":"1921-1928","abstract":"Flumes are specially shaped, engineered structures that have been used widely for measuring flow. Flumes are typically fabricated from aluminum or fiberglass; however, these types of flumes can be costly if purchased commercially and may lack machine precision if custom fabricated. This limits availability for widespread monitoring by smaller municipalities, engineering firms, or researchers with limited budgets. Using 3D printing technology (additive manufacturing) to produce flumes is very cost-effective, but variability between flumes and materials has not been tested, and discharge equations have not been developed for 3D printed flumes. In this study, a laboratory-scale setup was used to develop discharge equations for two types of 3D printed flumes (0.122 m HS flume and 0.102 m Palmer-Bowlus flume) made from two 3D printing materials: polylactic acid (PLA) and polyethylene terephthalate glycol modified (PETG). Variability between the same type of flume and between different materials for the same type of flume was analyzed to evaluate the consistency of the discharge equation with flumes of the same type. Eight models were developed to fit each dataset (PLA, PETG, and combined PLA and PETG) for both flume types and evaluated for goodness-of-fit and information criteria (AIC and BIC for model parsimony) to select the discharge equation for each flume type. Discharge equations were consistent for the same type of flume across each print and across different print materials. The discharge equations of 3D printed 0.122 m HS flumes and 0.102 m Palmer-Bowlus flumes are Q = 0.45624 × H2.351 and Q = 0.0001176 + 1.309 × (H - 0.0174625)2.235, respectively. The discharge equations of both flume types had R2adj values greater than 97% for the measured data of each individual flume. For hydraulic experimental modeling, this technique offers a new alternative that could enable a more sufficient and rapid model fabrication, especially for models that feature complex geometries. The present study thus evaluates the feasibility of applying 3D printing to fabricate scaled hydraulic experimental models for laboratory use. Various weir models were printed and compared to conventionally produced reference models in terms of the fabrication process, resulting discharge coefficients, and hydraulic performance. Results show that while being more cost-and time-effective during the fabrication process, properly 3D printed models were able to fulfill experimental requirements and deliver accurate results with a relative deviation less than 5% compared to conventionally fabricated models. The printing layer height was found to be the most critical parameter influencing the model’s final quality. Associated with the additive building approach, surface irregularities of 3D printed models were noted to be able to cause undesired nappe behavior, which might affect experimental results under certain conditions. To avoid such issues, a reduction of plotted layer heights or additional surface improvements could be helpful.
